strengths: The central idea—replacing pointwise fidelity with aggregate calibration of probability-integral-transform residuals—is intuitive, potentially useful, and easy to integrate into differentiable inverse-problem pipelines.
Experiments span Gaussian denoising, deconvolution, and Poisson PET reconstruction, and consistently illustrate stable late-iteration behavior compared with MSE/NLL.

The paper includes substantial implementation detail, numerical tail approximations, timing measurements, multiple noise levels and image resolutions, and candid discussion of non-identifiability and computational overhead.
The DIP and PET results suggest that the proposed objective can complement implicit or explicit regularization and reduce sensitivity to early stopping.
weaknesses: The objective discards measurement identity after sorting residual scores. Consequently, arbitrarily permuted or reassigned residual quantiles can attain the same loss while corresponding to very different signals. The paper acknowledges non-uniqueness but does not characterize how severe it is or establish conditions under which optimization selects an accurate reconstruction; this substantially weakens the claimed status of DC as a general data-fidelity replacement.

The theoretical treatment contains important gaps. Proposition B.2 assumes an effectively bounded logit derivative even though PIT values can approach 0 or 1, and the statement that tail values are negligible for Wasserstein-1 is not a justification. Its corollary also requires stronger control of the per-index Lipschitz constants. Moreover, the construction in Section 4.2 is called a “worst case” without proving any worst-case bound.

There are implementation inconsistencies: Algorithm 4's upper-tail Poisson expression uses -m log(q), whereas the preceding derivation gives -(m+1) log(q); additionally, setting q=max(y,0) permits log(0). These issues affect reproducibility and potentially gradients in the PET experiment.

For discrete Poisson observations, the naive PIT is not uniform. The authors show substantial deviation even for the clean PET sinogram, yet optimize toward a uniform target rather than using the exact randomized PIT or the empirically motivated discrete alternative. Thus the principal PET objective is misspecified, especially at low count levels.

The clipped-Gaussian treatment is an ad hoc linear smoothing and endpoint resampling scheme rather than the exact CDF or a rigorously derived randomized PIT. Its claimed smoothness is not established, and sensitivity to the ramp width and clamping thresholds is not evaluated.

The evaluation is too narrow for the broad claims: DIP uses only a handful of images and five seeds; PET uses a single simulated 2D phantom with no real data, varied anatomy, scanner effects, background/randoms, or noise-model mismatch. There are no comparisons to discrepancy-principle stopping, residual goodness-of-fit/whiteness methods, SURE-style selection, or other calibration-based objectives.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. DC-Adam is mainly compared with unregularized NLL-Adam and MLEM run far beyond their useful stopping points, while peak metrics use ground-truth-oracle iteration selection. The regularized experiment reports a single handcrafted prior and oracle-selected beta without repeated noise realizations or statistical testing.

Positioning against prior work is very limited. The paper does not adequately relate DC to classical discrepancy principles, residual analysis, goodness-of-fit tests, posterior predictive checks, or distribution-matching losses, making novelty and the appropriate baselines difficult to assess.

The anonymous code repository is promised only for a later discussion stage, so the current submission does not yet provide the resources needed to verify the stochastic loss, approximations, and reported experiments.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive alternative to pointwise data fidelity: probability-integral-transform scores are aggregated and matched to a reference distribution, directly targeting residual calibration rather than individual noisy observations.

The method is simple, differentiable almost everywhere, compatible with existing forward models and regularizers, and accompanied by pseudocode for Gaussian, clipped-Gaussian, and Poisson observations.

The experiments consistently illustrate the intended qualitative behavior: unlike MSE/NLL optimization, DC optimization does not progressively interpolate the observed noise in the tested DIP, deconvolution, and PET examples.
The appendices provide useful implementation details, additional noise levels and image sizes, visualizations of residual-score distributions, and computational timing measurements.
The authors candidly acknowledge that low DC loss does not identify the true signal and can correspond to reconstructions with substantial error.
weaknesses: The central criterion is only a necessary marginal calibration condition. It discards the association between residuals and measurement indices, spatial locations, and predicted values, so systematically incorrect or structured residuals can attain low loss. The paper acknowledges non-identifiability but does not provide conditions under which the proposed optimization reliably selects an accurate solution.

The theoretical support is weak and contains problematic statements. Proposition B.2 assumes a finite Lipschitz constant after the logit transform even though its derivative diverges at 0 and 1; the footnote that tail values are negligible does not establish the claimed pointwise bound. Corollary B.3 also appears to omit the finite-N empirical error term. More generally, the analysis does not prove the claimed reconstruction or stability advantages.

The Poisson experiments use the non-randomized PIT even though it is not uniformly distributed for discrete observations. The deviation is substantial at low count levels, precisely the regime used for the regularized PET experiment. Suggesting randomized PIT as future work does not validate the objective actually evaluated.

The experimental evidence is too narrow for the broad inverse-problem claims. DIP is evaluated principally on one image over five random initializations, with four additional images shown at selected noise settings. PET uses a single synthetic 2D BrainWeb phantom and apparently a single noise realization, without uncertainty estimates, real data, alternative phantoms, or robustness to noise-model mismatch.

Comparisons are limited to basic MSE/NLL, MLEM, and one handcrafted regularizer. There are no comparisons with residual-whiteness or discrepancy-principle methods, statistical goodness-of-fit objectives, modern DIP stopping criteria, or other calibration-based losses. Related-work positioning against these established ideas is correspondingly incomplete.

Several conclusions overstate the results. In PET, DC-Adam does not outperform the best early-stopped MLEM reconstruction; it mainly remains stable after reaching a somewhat worse error. The reported regularized PET advantage is modest and based on oracle selection of the regularization weight using ground truth.

Important design choices are not ablated, including fresh stochastic logistic reference samples versus deterministic quantiles, Wasserstein distance versus other goodness-of-fit discrepancies, the logit transform, sorting, tail approximations, and randomized treatment of discrete observations.
DC is computationally expensive at scale: at one million samples its reported forward pass is hundreds of times slower than MSE/NLL. No scalable approximation is demonstrated.

Reproducibility is incomplete because the promised anonymous code repository was not supplied with the manuscript, and some approximation thresholds and implementation-sensitive choices are not clearly reported.

Overall, the idea is interesting and the qualitative examples are promising, but the unresolved identifiability issue, incomplete theory, misspecified discrete-data objective, and limited baselines and datasets leave the main claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful idea: replace pointwise fidelity with aggregate calibration of probability-integral-transform scores. The qualitative optimization picture is compelling: DC behaves similarly to conventional fidelity far from a solution but stops rewarding interpolation of individual noise realizations near the data-consistent regime.

The experiments span three meaningfully different settings—1D deconvolution, deep-image-prior denoising, and Poisson PET reconstruction—and consistently illustrate reduced late-iteration noise fitting.

The DIP results show a practically valuable property: unlike MSE, DC remains stable over long optimization runs and therefore substantially reduces sensitivity to early stopping. Results across several noise levels, images, and random initializations support the phenomenon.

The PET experiments suggest that DC can complement explicit regularization rather than merely replacing it. DC+TV achieves a better reported noise-detail trade-off than NLL+TV and appears less sensitive to the regularization coefficient.

The paper is unusually candid about non-identifiability, measurement-independence requirements, discrete-noise complications, and computational overhead. It also provides extensive implementation pseudocode, supplementary experiments, and timing measurements.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not yet sufficiently broad or controlled for a top-tier acceptance. DIP is compared primarily with its original MSE objective rather than stronger stopping or regularization strategies, while PET uses a single synthetic BrainWeb setup and limited baselines. There are no repeated PET trials, statistical uncertainty estimates, real data, or comparisons with modern regularized reconstruction methods.

The central objective is non-identifying: many incorrect reconstructions can attain the same aggregate residual distribution. The paper acknowledges this and even constructs an estimate with twice the measurement-noise error, but provides no conditions explaining when optimization plus a given prior selects a good member of the equivalence class. Consequently, the empirical success may depend strongly on architecture, initialization, and optimization path.

The treatment of discrete Poisson noise is a significant unresolved issue. The experiments optimize the naive PIT against a uniform target even though the true Poisson PIT is not uniform. Figure F1 shows substantial mismatch at low count levels, precisely where the regularized PET experiment is conducted. Randomized PIT is discussed but not evaluated, so the PET objective is knowingly biased away from the ground truth.

Parts of the theoretical analysis are insufficiently rigorous. Proposition B.2 invokes a finite Lipschitz constant for the logit despite its derivative diverging near 0 and 1; Gaussian measurements have unbounded support, so the stated compact-interval argument does not establish the claimed bound. The assertion that tail values contribute negligibly to Wasserstein-1 is not justified, and the subsequent error bound therefore does not follow under the stated assumptions.

The paper does not ablate several consequential design choices, including stochastic samples versus deterministic logistic quantiles, reference-sample size, Wasserstein distance versus alternative calibration discrepancies, tail thresholds, endpoint randomization for clipped Gaussian data, or sensitivity to misspecified noise parameters and correlated measurements.

Experimental comparisons contain potential confounds. PET methods do not appear to receive fully matched constraints or optimization machinery, and the convex-hull mask is derived from phantom support information. Ground-truth-tuned early stopping and regularization strengths are used for conclusions without a practical model-selection protocol.

The related-work discussion is too narrow for the claimed foundational contribution. Connections to residual goodness-of-fit testing, discrepancy principles, residual whiteness, calibration objectives, and distribution-matching estimators need substantially deeper positioning to establish novelty.

Reproducibility is incomplete at review time because the anonymous code repository is promised only for the discussion period. Moreover, DC has substantial scaling cost: at one million measurements, its reported forward pass is hundreds of times slower than MSE/NLL due largely to sorting, which limits the claim that it is a straightforward practical replacement.
